strengths: The paper addresses an important practical problem and presents an intuitive three-stage pipeline combining data-augmented fine-tuning, self-training on successful generations, and GRPO with performance-scored exemplars.
The evaluation is nominally broad, covering all 250 KernelBench tasks and six GPU architectures, and includes component, sampling-strategy, and optimization-technique ablations.
The authors recognize reward-hacking risks, use more correctness inputs than prior KernelBench work, report quantiles in addition to means and maxima, and provide concrete case-study code.
weaknesses: The central evaluation appears fundamentally invalid because asynchronous work is not timed correctly. The Conv3D implementation launches the same F.conv3d operation on a private CUDA stream and returns immediately; Table 10 nevertheless attributes approximately 124x speedup to the stream alone, while Figure 4 explicitly describes “asynchronous GPU execution (no sync).” This measures submission rather than completed computation. The GRU implementation has the same problem, explaining the implausible 260–466x results that dominate the reported averages.

The supplied implementations contain additional correctness and executability defects. The Conv3D warm-up uses a 4x4x4 input with a 3x5x7 kernel and no padding, which is invalid. The GRU copies inputs on one stream and replays its graph on another without establishing a per-call dependency, returns a static output before replay completion, and attempts graph capture without the required warm-up. Several illustrative kernels also introduce races, out-of-bounds accesses, or changed output semantics.

There is complete task leakage: all 250 KernelBench tasks are used for SFT data generation and apparently throughout self-training and RL, then the same 250 tasks are used for evaluation. There is no held-out task, shape, or workload split, so the repeated claim of generalization to unseen kernels is unsupported. Cross-GPU testing only evaluates hardware transfer of the same memorized kernels.

Baseline comparisons are not controlled for search or compute budget. Vanilla models receive five attempts, whereas evolutionary and RL systems use unspecified numbers of generations and candidates. It is unclear whether CUDA-L1 results are single final-model generations or the best candidates accumulated during training. Important compiler and kernel-generation baselines are absent, and the prior system claimed to be a baseline is not clearly represented in the results table.

The work is not reproducible: it omits training iterations, group size, optimizer and learning rate, sampling settings, bucket width and temperature, GRPO coefficients, model-update details, hardware count, total compute, random seeds, per-task runtimes, generated kernels, code, data, and checkpoints. There are no independent training runs, confidence intervals, or synchronization-correct raw timing results.

The methodological novelty is limited to standard GRPO supplied with scored in-context exemplars, closely resembling evolutionary prompting plus parameter updates. Moreover, subtracting the common mean inside the softmax in Equation 1 cancels exactly and cannot alter selection probabilities as claimed. The text specifies two exemplars while the illustrated prompt contains four.

Prompt-only prohibitions and random-input tests do not adequately address reward hacking, fixed-shape specialization, caching, stream races, numerical tolerance, varied dtypes/layouts, or gradient semantics. The paper’s incorrect assertions that default-stream PyTorch convolutions repeatedly block the CPU and that a dedicated stream removes thousands of synchronization points further undermine the technical analysis. Consequently, the reported 17.7x mean and 449x peak speedups, and the conclusions derived from them, are unsupported.

Reproducibility is inadequate: essential SFT/GRPO hyperparameters, iteration and sample counts, bucket width and temperature, optimizer settings, correctness tolerances and input distributions, checkpoint details, and complete training compute are missing. No accessible code, model, or dataset link is provided.

Numerous internal inconsistencies undermine confidence. Table 5's counts imply rates such as 20.0%, 70.0%, 82.8%, and 90.4%, while the prose reports 22.4%, 66%, 88.4%, and 96%; it also falsely says every evolutionary baseline improves over 70% of tasks. The 120× case is variously called task 38 versus 83 and a transposed convolution despite using `Conv3d`.

Headline means are heavily influenced by benchmark-specific outliers and degenerate fixed-shape shortcuts; the primary median gain over the default baseline is only 1.42×. There are no confidence intervals or repeated end-to-end runs, and some shortcuts—such as returning the same preallocated output buffer—do not preserve general program semantics. Overall, these issues make the main quantitative claims unreliable rather than merely incomplete.

strengths: The manuscript addresses an important problem, and combining performance-scored exemplars with policy optimization is an intuitive approach to automated kernel optimization. The empirical scope is potentially valuable: 250 KernelBench workloads, several compilation baselines, five GPU architectures, and reporting of medians and percentiles in addition to means.

The authors show awareness of GPU benchmarking noise through dedicated devices, paired randomized execution, long measurement windows, and repeat-device verification. The discussion of discovered reward-hacking behaviors is unusually candid.
The paper attempts useful component comparisons covering SFT, self-training, vanilla GRPO, fixed-model evolutionary search, and several exemplar-selection strategies.
weaknesses: The central evaluation is fundamentally contaminated. SFT data are constructed from all 250 KernelBench tasks, no held-out split is specified for later training stages, and the headline results are reported on those same tasks. The protocol therefore measures task-specific optimization/search on the benchmark rather than generalization of a learned optimizer. The repeated claim of transfer to unseen kernels is unsupported; testing the same kernels on other GPUs establishes hardware portability, not task generalization.

The appendix directly contradicts the claimed correctness validation. In the LSTM case, the reference returns state[0], whereas the purported optimized implementation returns self.fc(last_out), with a different shape and semantics. It also initializes c0 independently even though the reference overwrites c0 with h0. Such code could not pass even a basic shape comparison, casting doubt on the evaluation pipeline and reported 3.4× result.

The case studies contain further major inconsistencies: Section 5.3 attributes the 120× result to Level-2 Task 38 and a transposed-convolution/pooling pipeline, while Table 7 and Appendix B instead describe Task 83, using Conv3d, GroupNorm, minimum, clamp, and dropout. Table 5 also disagrees with its analysis: for example, 226/250 is 90.4%, not the claimed 96%, and 186/250 is 74.4%, not 82.4%.

Reward hacking remains unresolved. The checking model reportedly detects only above 60% of attacks, no exhaustive audit of final kernels is reported, and the proposed stream synchronization assumes that arbitrary model-created streams can be identified. The appendix nevertheless presents returning work on custom asynchronous streams as an optimization, closely resembling the timing exploit discussed earlier.

The technical novelty and formulation are weak. Contrastive-RL is essentially standard GRPO with scored implementations inserted into the prompt. Subtracting the same global mean from every bucket logit in Equation 1 cannot change the softmax distribution, contrary to the claimed sampling benefit. Likewise, interpreting a 1.5 threshold on standardized rewards as a 1.5× speedup is mathematically incorrect.

Reproducibility is inadequate for a 671B-parameter training study: learning rates, optimizers, batch and group sizes, iteration counts, sampling temperature, bucket widths, KL and clipping coefficients, model-update details, random seeds, inference-selection protocol, total samples, and computational cost are mostly absent. No accessible code, checkpoints, generated kernels, or CUDA-Graph artifact link is supplied.

Comparisons are not compute-matched. Vanilla models receive five trials, evolutionary-search budgets are unspecified, and CUDA-L1's training/search budget is unreported despite 30-minute candidate measurements. There are no independent training runs, confidence intervals, or direct experimental comparison with the strongest related KernelBench system cited by the paper.

The 3.12× mean is dominated by extreme, benchmark-specific outliers; the median is only 1.42×. The highlighted 120× case exploits fixed constants to return a preallocated zero tensor, while the 64× case is a straightforward algebraic PyTorch rewrite. These are useful specializations but do not substantiate broad claims about discovering general CUDA optimization principles.

The manuscript is not submission-ready: it contains an unresolved citation placeholder, malformed text such as “latexIn,” numerous grammatical errors and terminology inconsistencies, and overlapping or poorly placed table material. More importantly, these presentation problems accompany substantive contradictions rather than being merely cosmetic.
